title: Memorization Through Compression: The Adversarial Compression Ratio
one_liner: Memorization happens when a model can output training data from a much shorter prompt than the data itself.
lead: When a model memorizes training data, it stores information in its weights. A clever way to detect this is to ask: what is the shortest prompt that makes the model spit out that training data? If the prompt is much shorter than the data, the model must have stored it. This paper proposes Adversarial Compression Ratio (ACR) to measure memorization at scale.

paras: To know if a model memorized a training example, you normally have to retrain the entire model twice: once with that example and once without it, then compare how well it performs on that example. This is called counterfactual memorization. For a language model with billions of weights, this is prohibitively expensive.

Existing definitions of memorization are also vague. One says a model memorized something if you can prompt it with part of the training data and it completes it exactly. But what about text that appears multiple times in training? What about text similar to training data but not exact? The definitions lack a principled way to distinguish storage from generalization.

A beginner might think: just check if the model can output the exact string. But this doesn't tell you if the model learned the words or merely reproduced them word-for-word from memory. You need a precise, practical measure.

callout.html: Measure memorization by finding the shortest prompt that forces the model to output that training example.

steps.text: For a training example, what is the shortest prompt that makes the model output it exactly?
Use GCG algorithm to find prompts that trigger the training example, starting short and growing.
Calculate the ratio of training-example length to shortest-prompt length.
High ratio means memorized (stored in weights); low ratio means learned (generalized).
Use the ratio to audit what a model memorized and measure success of unlearning.

paras: The paper changes how we measure memorization. Instead of retraining models, it focuses on one simple object: the length of the shortest prompt that forces output of a training example. This single number—prompt length—becomes the yardstick.

hidden.name: Compression Ratio (ACR)
paras: The hidden quantity is the Compression Ratio, which is simply the length of the training example divided by the length of the shortest prompt that triggers it. If you can compress a 100-token example into a 10-token prompt, the ratio is 10. A high ratio means the model has squeezed information into its weights; a low ratio (near 1) means it learned to generalize.

The paper measures this by running GCG (a search algorithm) to find the shortest prompt iteratively. It starts with a guess, runs the search for a budget of steps, and if the prompt still doesn't work, it adds tokens and tries again. The final successful prompt's length is the denominator.

heat.caption: Darker means that prompt token is more critical to triggering the exact training output.

reads.html: A memorized phrase is one where the model has stored it as a tight pattern. A short prompt triggers it because the weights already know exactly what should come next.
Given a model M and a training sample y, ACR(M, y) is defined as the length of y divided by the length of the shortest prompt p such that M(p) outputs y exactly.

paras: Memorization works because the model stores specific sequences in its weights. When the weights encode the exact tokens of a training example, only a few trigger tokens are needed to recall the rest. The model has done the information compression work during training; the prompt just needs to hit the right 'key' in memory.

Generalization works differently. When a model learns a concept (e.g., the structure of English), it distributes that knowledge across many weights. No short prompt can extract the exact training sentence because the model is reconstructing it from general rules, not replaying stored data. Each output token requires multiple weights to cooperate, so nothing is memorized as a rigid sequence.

The search algorithm (GCG) automates this detection. It treats prompt construction as an optimization problem: find the prompt that makes the model output the target text, using as few tokens as possible. If a short prompt exists, memorization is happening. If only a long prompt works (or no prompt works), the model generalized.

stages.s: Pick a training example (e.g., a Wikipedia paragraph)
Run GCG search: test random prompts, score how close the output matches the target
Keep the best prompts; grow or shrink them; repeat until finding shortest trigger
Measure compression ratio: example length divided by shortest prompt length
High ratio signals memorization, low ratio signals generalization

math.words: compression ratio equals length of training example divided by length of the shortest prompt that produces it
math.equation: ACR(M, y) = len(y) / len(p_min),  where p_min is the shortest prompt such that M(p_min) = y
symbols: a training example (a sequence of tokens)
the shortest prompt that causes M to output y exactly
number of tokens in the training example
number of tokens in the minimal prompt

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Training example: 'Paris is the capital of France and sits on the Seine River.' = 13 tokens.
Search finds shortest prompt that triggers it: 'Paris capital' = 2 tokens.
Ratio of 6.5 is high, indicating memorization. The model can compress a 13-token fact into a 2-token reminder.
Contrast: if the shortest prompt were 11 tokens, ACR = 13/11 = 1.18, nearly no compression, suggesting generalization.

math.note: The higher the ratio, the tighter the memorization. A ratio near 1 means prompt and output are nearly the same length—no compression, no memorization.

charts.title: Counterfactual memorization (old method)
charts.note: Exact but prohibitively expensive; requires retraining the entire model for each sample.

charts.title: Adversarial Compression Ratio (this paper)
charts.note: Approximate but practical; runs forward passes and searches, no model retraining needed.

items.html: If you feed the algorithm text that was never in training (e.g. news from after training), the GCG search may still find a short prompt by accident. The paper shows this is rare: it never observed non-training text compress in their experiments.

Famous quotes that appear in paraphrased form in training may not compress well using the exact quote. The compression ratio conflates exact memorization with paraphrase variants. The paper measures this as separate: famous quotes compress with ratio 1.17, but paraphrases only 0.68.

items.b: Search timeout misses very short prompts.
items.html: GCG has a time budget. If the true minimal prompt requires deeper search, the algorithm stops and reports a longer prompt than actually exists, inflating the compression ratio artificially.

items.b: Done right: randomness and repeated searches.
items.html: Run the search multiple times with different random seeds; report the shortest prompt found. Use adaptive time budgets (more time for longer prompts) to avoid timeout bias.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small language model (or use a pretrained one like Pythia-1.4B) and a dataset with known training examples. For each example, run GCG to find the shortest trigger prompt. Collect the compression ratios. Then artificially insert new sentences into the dataset and retrain slightly, or fetch text never in training (e.g. recent news, text external to the training set). Run the same search. Plot histograms of compression ratios for three groups: original training, retraining data, and external text.
demo.metric_eq: ACR_train = average compression ratio for original training examples. ACR_external = average for external text. Success: ACR_train > 1.5 and ACR_external < 1.1.
demo.closing: The gap between training and external-text compression ratios proves memorization is real and measurable without retraining.
